stories.headline: Iran president meets PM Modi, seeks help to end war
stories.title: Iran president meets PM Modi, seeks help to end war
stories.summary: Prime Minister Modi convened with Iranian President Pezeshkian to advance discussions on fortifying trade connections between their nations. Both leaders acknowledged the critical role of maritime freedom and trade in the region. They also discussed the ongoing situations in West Asia, focusing on the importance of Chabahar port collaboration. President Pezeshkian encouraged India to mediate for peace, underscoring their shared dedication to enhancing bilateral economic cooperation.

stories.headline: Bihar CM urges Union Minister of Jal Shakti to accelerate irrigation and flood control projects
stories.title: Bihar CM urges Union Minister of Jal Shakti to accelerate irrigation and flood control projects
stories.summary: Samrat Choudhary urged for the early approval and release of central assistance for pending irrigation and flood management projects announced in the Union Budget, including the Kosi-Mechi Inter-State River Link Project.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'union budget' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary on Monday (August 31, 2026) urged Union Minister of Jal Shakti C.R. Patil to accelerate water resource, irrigation, and flood management projects concerning Bihar.

Accompanied by Bihar Deputy Chief Minister and Water Resources Minister Vijay Kumar Choudhary in Delhi, the CM informed Mr. Patil that the Union Budget 2024-25 had announced financial assistance for several schemes in the irrigation and water resources sector for Bihar, including the Kosi-Mechi Inter-State River Link Project (costing ₹11,500 crore).
He added, Bihar government had submitted Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) worth ₹16,339.18 crore to the Central Government; however, only two projects have received approval so far.

The Kosi-Mechi Inter-State River Link Project, valued at approximately ₹3,652.56 crore, will help to expand irrigation facilities in North Bihar by making better use of the surplus water from the Kosi basin.
Provisions totalling ₹965.41 crore have been made for the project’s first phase—₹395.41 crore for the 2025-26 financial year and ₹570 crore for 2026-27.
However, only ₹156.745 crore has been received so far.
Mr. Choudhary urged the early release of the remaining funds for the first phase and the approval of the Detailed Project Report (DPR) for the second phase.
He also raised the issue of the early release of the funds for Sikrahana Right Embankment construction scheme, in which the central share is ₹125.08 crore.

The status of other schemes proposed under the Union Budget 2024-25 was reviewed which includes three irrigation projects with an estimated cost of ₹5,951.45 crore and 15 flood management projects with an estimated cost of ₹3,896.14 crore, all of which are currently under consideration at various levels within the Ministry of Jal Shakti.
Progress on the Extension, Renovation, and Modernisation (ERM) of the Western Kosi Canal Project—announced in the Union Budget 2025-26—was also reviewed.
The Bihar government has submitted a DPR worth ₹8,338.89 crore for this project to the Central Water Commission (CWC).
Anticipating central assistance, the state government has already commenced work on the first phase, costing ₹3,484.24 crore, using its own resources.

stories.headline: When the Himalayas Speak, Kashmir Must Listen
stories.title: When the Himalayas Speak, Kashmir Must Listen
stories.summary: The Himalayas have always stood before us like an ancient promise—majestic, snow-covered and seemingly eternal. They have given birth to rivers, sustained civilisations, shaped cultures and supported millions of lives. For generations, we have looked at their peaks with awe, rarely imagining that beneath that silence the mountains themselves could be changing. Today, however, the Himalayas are speaking in a different language—in melting glaciers, unstable slopes, cloudbursts, landslides, avalanches and rivers that can turn destructive within minutes. The recent catastrophe in the Nepal–Tibet Himalayan region should therefore not be viewed merely as a tragedy unfolding somewhere far away. For Kashmir, and for the entire Himalayan belt, it should be understood as a warning. The question is no longer whether the Himalayas are changing. The question is whether we are prepared to change with them. The Himalayas do not recognise political boundaries. A glacier does not know where one country ends, and another begins. A river does not carry a passport. A landslide does not stop at a border. Nature follows geology, gravity, water and weather—not the lines human beings have drawn on maps. What happens in Nepal can therefore offer lessons to Kashmir. What happens in Uttarakhand can concern Himachal Pradesh. What happens in the high mountains of Tibet can eventually affect valleys and river systems far beyond the immediate point of origin. The Himalayas are one interconnected ecological and geological system, and their risks are interconnected as well. Kashmir has already received its warnings The devastating floods of 2014 remain one of the Valley's most painful memories. We have witnessed cloudbursts, landslides, avalanches and extreme weather events. We have seen roads disappear, bridges collapse and communities become isolated. Yet our response to disasters too often follows the same cycle: catastrophe, rescue, compensation, reconstruction—and eventually forgetfulness. We cannot afford to forget anymore The changing climate has added a new dimension to Himalayan vulnerability. Glaciers are retreating, snow patterns are changing, permafrost is becoming unstable and glacial lakes are evolving. These changes can create cascading hazards. A sudden collapse of ice or rock can displace water, trigger a flood or debris flow, block a river and create conditions for an even larger disaster downstream. A peaceful mountain stream can become a raging torrent within minutes For Kashmir, this means that glaciers and high-altitude lakes can no longer be regarded merely as scenic features. They are part of a complex and changing risk landscape. Vulnerable glaciers, glacial lakes and mountain slopes need continuous scientific monitoring through satellites, ground surveys, weather stations and hydrological observations. Early-warning systems must be strengthened, and the information generated by scientists must reach local communities in time. Because a warning that arrives after the flood is not a warning. It is equally important to rethink what we mean by development in the mountains. Kashmir needs roads, bridges, hospitals, schools, electricity, communication and tourism infrastructure. Its people need employment and economic opportunity. Development cannot and should not stop. But development that ignores the character of the mountain can ultimately become an invitation to disaster. A Himalayan slope is not a plain. A riverbank is not automatically safe land. A wetland is not wasteland. A forest is not merely a source of timber. And a glacier is not simply a tourist attraction. We have become accustomed to asking: Can we build here? Perhaps the more important question is: Should we build here? That distinction could save lives. Every mountain has a carrying capacity. Every river has a floodplain. Every wetland has a function. Every forest helps stabilise the landscape. When we ignore these natural systems, we may gain land for construction but lose nature's own protection against disasters. The Jhelum is a particularly important reminder for Kashmir. It is not merely a river flowing through the Valley; it is part of an intricate network of lakes, wetlands, tributaries and flood channels that regulate water. The floods of 2014 demonstrated the consequences of disrupting this natural system. A river may remain quiet for years, but it never forgets its floodplain. If wetlands are encroached upon, drainage channels obstructed and flood-prone areas converted into settlements, we are not eliminating flood risk. We are merely storing it for another day. Tourism requires similar caution. Kashmir's extraordinary landscapes attract visitors from across the country and the world, but beauty can sometimes conceal danger. A tourist standing beside a mountain stream may have no idea that a cloudburst or sudden event upstream can transform that stream into a deadly torrent. A traveller entering a remote valley may not know how quickly a landslide can cut off the only road. Tourism must therefore be accompanied by a safety architecture—weather alerts, evacuation routes, emergency shelters, trained guides, communication systems and clear protocols for extreme weather. Adventure should never mean ignorance of risk Another critical lesson is that Himalayan disasters rarely remain isolated. An earthquake can trigger a landslide; a landslide can block a river; a blocked river can form a temporary lake; the collapse of that natural barrier can send a destructive surge downstream. This possibility of cascading disasters demands a new approach to disaster management. Floods, earthquakes, landslides, avalanches and cloudbursts cannot be treated as completely separate risks. The Himalayas do not operate in government departments, and neither should disaster preparedness. Kashmir needs integrated mountain-risk planning involving geologists, glaciologists, hydrologists, meteorologists, engineers, environmental experts, disaster-management authorities and local communities. But science must not remain confined to laboratories and government files. It must reach the last village. People living below vulnerable slopes or along flood-prone rivers should know where they will go when an alarm sounds, which route is safe and where the nearest shelter is located. Schools and hospitals in vulnerable areas should have evacuation plans. Local communities should be trained because, in the first hours of a disaster, ordinary people are often the first responders. Technology can detect danger. Preparedness saves lives The entire Himalayan region also needs greater cooperation in disaster preparedness. India, Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet and other Himalayan regions may be separated by political boundaries, but they share mountains, weather systems, rivers and ecological vulnerabilities. Political borders may divide territories. They cannot divide an ecosystem Information about glaciers, extreme rainfall, river levels, landslides and other hazards should therefore be shared as rapidly as possible. A Himalayan early-warning system must ultimately be guided by the geography of risk, not merely by political maps. The deeper issue, however, is our attitude towards nature. For decades, concrete has been treated as a symbol of progress. More roads, more buildings, more tunnels and more commercial infrastructure are often equated with development. But the Himalayas are young, fragile and geologically active. Engineering suitable for the plains cannot simply be imposed upon the mountains. The Himalayas do not need to be conquered. They need to be understood. We cannot prevent every earthquake. We cannot stop every cloudburst. We cannot freeze every glacier. But we can decide where we build, how we build and how much pressure we place on fragile mountain ecosystems. We can protect wetlands. We can enforce building codes. We can monitor glaciers. We can establish early-warning systems. We can regulate construction in high-risk zones. We can make tourism safer. We can prepare communities before disaster strikes. And above all, we can learn. The recent tragedy in Nepal and Tibet should therefore become more than an occasion for expressing sympathy. It should become an opportunity for Himalayan introspection. How many warnings do we need before we change? How many floods must destroy roads before we build differently? How many wetlands must disappear before we recognise their value? How many mountain slopes must collapse before we understand that every slope has a limit? These are uncomfortable questions, but they must be asked. Kashmir's rivers, lakes, forests, glaciers and mountains are not merely scenic assets. They are life-support systems. If we destroy them, we are not simply losing beauty; we are weakening our own protection. The Himalayas have given us water, forests, fertile valleys, livelihoods, culture and spiritual traditions for thousands of years. The least we can offer in return is restraint. The mountains have stood silently for millions of years. But silence should never be mistaken for consent. Today they are speaking—in the cracking glacier, the unstable slope, the swollen river and the sudden roar of water. Kashmir must listen. The entire Himalayan region must listen Because we may not be able to prevent every natural hazard, but with foresight, science and preparedness, we can prevent many natural hazards from becoming human catastrophes. And perhaps that is the message the mountains are sending us: The Himalayas may survive our mistakes. The real question is whether we will. (The writer can be reached at: sanjaypanditasp@gmail.com)

stories.headline: India looks to expand Iran trade amid US curbs
stories.title: India looks to expand Iran trade amid US curbs
stories.summary: New Delhi: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Bishkek, in what was their maiden in-person engagement since the war and discussed expanding and diversifying trade ties and reiterated New Delhi's commitment "to strengthening India's long-standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors"."Met President Masoud Pezeshkian in Bishkek. Reiterated our commitment to strengthening India's long-standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors. We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come," Modi wrote on X following his meeting with Pezeshkian. This statement signals India's willingness to widen trade partnership with Iran amid the US sanctions on the Persian Gulf state.During the meeting, Modi also called for freedom of navigation and protecting the lives of seafarers in the backdrop of the challenges faced by India amid the volatility in West Asia. Since the war, Modi and the Iranian President had held three telephone conversations on the Hormuz Strait navigation and the conflict situation.Modi informed Pezeshkian of India's readiness to closely cooperate with Iran in multilateral organisations, including BRICS and SCO, and conveyed that he looked forward to welcoming President Pezeshkian to India for the BRICS summit here on September 12-13, according to an official.It is understood that the two leaders discussed Iran's position on the war that it wants to be reflected in the BRICS declaration and India's views on BRICS unity.The two leaders discussed various aspects of bilateral ties, including Iran's energy exports to India and retaining India's interests in the Chabahar Port through an arrangement with Tehran. They discussed the recent developments in the West Asia conflict and shared perspectives on the evolving situation, according to a readout by the Ministry of External Affairs.

stories.headline: Bridging the link between science and ground reality
stories.title: Bridging the link between science and ground reality
stories.summary: SHEIKH ANEAUS The latest catastrophe in Nepal serves as a terrible illustration. In order to reconstruct what transpired high in the mountains, scientists are currently analyzing hydrological observations, satellite pictures, and more data. However, the incident happened so fast that community downstream had very little time to react. Experts have since stressed the importance of better satellite monitoring, real-time river monitoring, quicker detection of blockages and stronger early-warning systems to help reduce the impact of such events. The problem is not always a deficiency of scientific data. There are instances when the information is available but the connection between monitoring, research, and action is insufficient. Scientific studies are giving us clearer picture of how the landscape is changing around us. Satellites are tracking glaciers and lakes, field expeditions are carried out to record changes in mountainous regions, weather stations are collecting observations, and researchers are using these observations to better understand natural hazards such as floods and landslides. But collecting information is only one part of the job. The true worth of research is demonstrated when the data aids in decision-making. In areas where infrastructure and people can be rapidly impacted by environmental changes, this becomes particularly crucial. A change seen in a high-altitude lake or glacier could start as a scientific observation. When that information is coupled to the settlements, roads, bridges, power projects, and other facilities that are located downstream, its significance becomes much more evident. That link between research and application needs to remain strong. This does not suggest that government organizations and researchers operate independently. Environmental risks are already being monitored and understood by a number of entities. The Geological Survey of India, the Central Water Commission, the National Disaster Management Authority, ISRO and its National Remote Sensing Center, the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology, and other scientific organizations are working on various aspects of mountain hazards, monitoring, and disaster preparedness. Additionally, the Central Water Commission has created a risk-indexing method for glacial lakes, and it is working with organizations like ISRO and C-DAC to build early warning systems. These initiatives offer a critical base. The next step is to assure that the information produced through them can move smoothly between those who generate it and those who need to act on it. A change in a glacier, lake, or mountain slope could be detected by a researcher. An organization in charge of disaster management might need to determine if that change needs to be addressed right now. It may be necessary for a local government to know which routes or settlements might be impacted. The infrastructure department may need to know if a project or bridge is located in a potentially dangerous area. Each of these may only be a part of the picture. Combining those components can provide a much clearer picture of the true danger. This is where regular information exchange becomes important. Researchers require access to relevant ground data, while implementing agencies want timely access to scientific findings. Similarly, in-situ observations can also help researchers understand changes that might not be apparent from satellite imagery alone. For instance, a satellite image indicates that a lake has expanded. That information becomes much more useful when it is combined with the condition of the surrounding slopes, the drainage of the lake and the location of settlements and infrastructure in downstream areas. This also holds true for other hazards. When a rainfall forecast is combined with the data pertaining to slopes prone to landslides, it becomes more valuable. When highways, bridges, and settlements are included, in a flood map it is much more helpful. Glacier change when connected with information on the drainage system beneath it, is a value addition. In many cases, the information is already available, but bringing it all together is the challenge. This doesn't always mean that new systems need to be developed. When data from many sources is combined and updated on a regular basis, monitoring programs, databases, and communication channels can become more beneficial. The important question is how effectively these different sources of information can work together when a situation develops. An official might want a far more straightforward response, even though a research report might include a thorough scientific analysis: Is there a change? Where's it? What might take place? Which regions are at risk? What should I watch after this? That does not imply eliminating uncertainty or reducing the science to a few numbers. It is quite the reverse. Making wise choices requires an awareness of both the known and the unknown. Closer observation or a ground monitoring may be the best course of action if the information at hand is insufficient to assess if a change is hazardous. It could be necessary to do additional modeling if a potential flood pathway is unclear. Authorities don't need to wait for all the answers to scientific questions to start planning if a vulnerable location is already known. This strategy can assist prevent unwarranted worry and complacency. Scientific data on glaciers, rainfall, rivers, terrain and past disasters can be combined with information on settlements and infrastructure to identify areas where environmental hazards may affect people. This can help guide infrastructure planning, evacuation routes and field monitoring, making research part of regular planning rather than a response after disasters. Local communities can also provide useful information, as they often notice changes in water levels, slopes, cracks and streams before they are recorded officially. This kind of observation cannot replace scientific monitoring, but they can add another layer of information. This also applies to early warning systems. Instrument installation is crucial, but an alert is only helpful if someone understands what it signifies and what needs to be done. Communities need to know exactly where to go, which routes to take, and how fast they might need to react. Therefore, preparation must start long in advance of an emergency. Identifying susceptible areas, comprehending potential risks, inspecting vital infrastructure, enhancing communication routes, and determining ahead of time who is in charge of what should all be part of it. This process can be greatly facilitated by stronger relationships between researchers and implementing authorities. Researchers can help identify emerging risks and explain what the available evidence means. Government departments can identify the information they need for planning and response. Local authorities and communities can provide information from the ground level. It should work both ways. Additionally, it should occur on a regular basis rather than just in the immediate aftermath of a calamity. A risk assessment completed a few years ago might not accurately reflect current conditions since environmental variables vary over time. Thus, frequent updates are just as crucial as the original evaluation. Creating more meetings or paperwork shouldn't be the goal. It ought to be to better utilize the data that is already being produced. Examples of research being beneficial outside of academia include a satellite image that prompts a field inspection, a field observation that enhances a risk map, a hazard map that modifies an infrastructure design, or an early warning that allows people enough time to evacuate to safety. We have the chance to accomplish this more successfully than in the past thanks to the expanding availability of satellite data, enhanced computation, better monitoring systems, and field observations. However, technology by itself won't bridge the divide. A habit of exchanging knowledge, posing pertinent questions, and maintaining open lines of communication between those who research a hazard and those who must prepare for it is what are required. Environmental risks can't always be avoided, and it's not always possible to foresee when they will occur. However, when information is accessible early and handled appropriately, their effects are frequently reduced. The goal should not simply be to produce more research. It should be to make the research we already have easier to share, understand and use. For downstream communities, the value of this work is quite simple. It means knowing when something has changed above them, understanding whether they may be at risk, and receiving a warning early enough to move themselves and their families to safety. Monitoring cannot prevent every flood, landslide or other mountain hazard. But timely information can give people something very important - time. Time to leave, time to close a road, time to move equipment, time to warn others and, most importantly, time to save lives. That is why bringing research and implementation closer together matters. It is not only about understanding how the landscape is changing. It is about making sure that what we learn reaches the people at the helm before the hazard reaches them. (The Author is a PhD in Geoinformatics. Feedback: sheikh.aneaus19@gmail.com)

stories.headline: India needs to raise investment rate to 34-35% of GDP for faster growth: Economist Surjit Bhalla
stories.title: India needs to raise investment rate to 34-35% of GDP for faster growth: Economist Surjit Bhalla
stories.summary: India's current investment-to-GDP ratio of around 28-30% would support long-term growth of about 6.5%, says economist Surjit Bhalla
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India's economy grew 7.8% in the first quarter of FY27.
"The most important policy that has been tried and tested in India and every other country in the world is that the investment rate," Bhalla said while speaking to news agency ANI.
He said India would need to raise the investment rate to around 34-35% of GDP to accelerate growth.
"Now, some years you get 7%, some years you get 7.5, some years, we get even 8," Bhalla said.
The noted economist pointed to the 2004-2013 period, when India sustained an investment rate of around 34% and recorded higher economic growth.
Bhalla said the effectiveness of investment also depends on global conditions.
"If global conditions are very favorable, then you may want that you can achieve a higher growth rate with a lower rate of investment," he said.
"But if the global conditions are as they are now and may even get worse, then you definitely need to step up the investment rate."
According to Bhalla, India's overall investment rate had remained relatively high, but its composition had changed sharply.
Private investment, he said, has declined by around 5-7 percentage points since 2011-12.
"We've had a higher investment rate.
